rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Setup 3 Gameplay 4 Scoring 5 End of Game 6 Variants 6.1 Cities & Knights 6.1.1 Event Dice 6.1.2 Cities 6.1.3 Variants Objective Get resources to buy various buildings and development cards, and try to be the first player to reach 10 points (or 13 in case of City & Knights) Setup The board consists of hills (brick), forest (lumber), mountains (ore), fields (grain), pasture (wool) and a desert (nothing) at random places. Each terrain except the desert has a number of 2-12 on it. The desert starts with the robber on it. Each player places 2 settlements and 1 road next to each settlement on the board, then they receive resources for each terrain around the second settlement. Gameplay Rolling for resource production (obligatory): On your turn, roll 2 dice and calculate the sum. The terrains with that number produce resources for all players who have settlements or cities next to them (if the robber isn't blocking them): 1 resource per settlement and 2 per city. If you roll a 7, no one gets any resources and players with 8 resources or more must discard half of them (rounded down). You must move the robber to a new terrain and steal 1 random resource from a player who has a settlement or city next to that terrain. Trading (optional): during your turn you can trade resources with all other players ( domestic trade ) with the bank ( maritime trade ) at the standard rate of 4 identical resources for 1 or at a preferential rate of a harbour if you have a settlement next to it. Building (optional): finally, you can build roads and settlements, upgrade settlements to cities or purchase a development card by paying the resources needed. Roads must connect to the initial settlements and cost 1 brick + 1 lumber (worth 0 points) Settlements must be connected by roads to existing settlements (except at start) and cost 1 brick + 1 lumber + 1 wool + 1 grain (worth 1 point) Cities replace an existing settlement and cost 3 ore + 2 grain (worth 2 points) Development cards (unavailable in Cities & Knights) cost 1 ore + 1 wool + 1 grain and include 14 Knight cards that allow to move the robber to another terrain and steal a resource 2 Road Building cards allowing extra roads to be built 2 Year of Plenty cards providing two free resources of choice 2 Monopoly cards giving all other players that help gathering resources or building road•s 5 Victory Point cards You can play a development card at any time during your turn, even before rolling the dice, as long as it was bought on a previous turn and is not a victory card. Scoring Settlements : each is worth 1 victory point . Cities : each is worth 2 victory points (1 Point from the settlement + 1). Victory Point cards : some development cards are worth 1 victory point . They are kept hidden until you have sufficent points to win. Controlling the Merchant figure grants you 1 Victory Point. Largest Army : the player who has played the most knight cards at any time (at least 3) gets the largest army card which is worth 2 points . No largest army in C&K. Longest Road : the player with the longest continuous road at any time (at least 5 segments) gets the longest road card which is worth 2 points . If there is a tie, the original owner keeps the achievement cards . End of Game If a player has 10 or more victory points during their turn (including victory points cards), they reveal them and the game ends with their victory. For Catan Cities & Knights, a player needs 13 or more victory points to win. Variants Easy Start: Players reroll any 7s they obtain in their first 2 turns. With the Cities & Knights expansion, the event dice is not rolled during these turns as well. Friendly Robber (Base Game only): The robber may not move to a terrain that is adjacent to a settlement of a player with only 2 victory points. If there is no valid terrain, the robber moves to the desert and the resource card cannot be taken from such players. Cities & Knights Event Dice An additional event dice is rolled each turn. If it shows a ship (3 faces), the barbarian ship moves 1 space closer to Catan. If it reaches the last space (7th), the barbarians attack. If it shows a coloured figure (yellow/grey/green) , not the black ship, players receive a progress card if the color of the figure and the red dice match their chart. Red dice match depends on your city improvement, eg if You have a Science (green) city improvement of level 1, you can see the small red dice icon with 1 and 2 at your city improvement sign. This means whenever the red dice shows 1 or 2, AND the 3rd dice shows the green figure, you automatically receive one progress card. Each player can have up to 4 Progress Cards at a time. Victory Point cards are immediately played and do not count. Others can be played similar to Development cards. When the barbarians attack, they have 1 strength per city/metropolis owned by all players; The defending army have strength equal to the value of all active knights. If the barbarians are stronger, they pillage a city of the player with the lowest value of active knights, reducing it to a settlement. This also destroys any city walls under it. If the defending army is equal or stronger, the player with the highest value of active knights (non-tied) gains a "Defender of Catan" victory point card, which is worth 1 victory point . If there is a tie, the tied players gain a progress card each instead. Regardless of the result, the barbarian ship is reset and all knights become inactive. Cities When a city produces wool/lumber/ore, replaces a resource they produce with a commodity (cloth/paper/coin) instead. Two new items can be built: City Walls must be under an existing city without one and cost 2 brick (worth 0 points). A player can have at most 3 city walls, and each increases the maximum number of cards they can safely hold when a 7 is rolled by 2. Knights must be connected by roads and cost 1 wool + 1 ore (worth 0 points). They start inactive at value 1, but they can be promoted with 1 wool + 1 ore (+1 value, up to 2) or activated with 1 grain. Active Knights may perform 1 action on your turn regardless of strength. This can be moving it along your roads to another intersection, moving it onto a weaker opponent knight (forcing it to move or removing it), or chasing away a robber adjacent to it (as per playing a knight). They become inactive afterwards. Cities can be developed in Trade (yellow)/Politics (grey)/Science (green) by paying 1 cloth/coin/paper per improvement level. The 3rd improvement provides a power each: trade 2 of the same commodity for a resource once per turn (Trade); may promote knights to value 3 (Politics); take any resource if no resources are gained and no robbers (Science). The first player who reach the 4th improvement in each area may place a Metropolis on a city. They are worth 4 victory points each and are immune to barbarians. Variants Nasty Battles: When the barbarians land, starting from the active player, each player declares the amount of their own active knights they would commit to defending Catan. Knight Errant: Before rolling the dice, a player may use an active knight to chase away the robber, as per playing a knight in base Catan.

---

This is an expansion for CATAN. Players can build shipping lanes, which are very similar to roads. Additionally, the game comes with many different water-hex-heavy variant setups. The English version (CATAN Studio) should only be used with the English base game, instead of the German one (Kosmos), because of matching components. The Kosmos German version should only be used with the German base game. Additionally, several different editions exist; 5th edition is the most recent. Editions should only be used with same edition, otherwise the purchase of adapter kit is required.

Part of the Catan Series.

This game requires CATAN.  Ideally, using the same publisher and edition of the game.
community_text:
[Rating: 2/10] Don't bother.  The new additions simply don't add much to the game beyond playtime.  It feels like the original, with unnecessary distracting crap thrown in.  The epitome of what I DON'T want an expansion to be.  [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/926]Cities & Knights[/url] is a much better expansion.

[Rating: 2/10] The more but smaller islands provide a bigger but more spread map, which results in more drawbacks than it's worth: * more cities border the sea => less efficiency/resource-income => slower start * cities further apart => more cost to connect * players are more spread => less tension in getting certain spots  All this combines into a longer game that has less player interaction. The other expansions offer more variety in gameplay with less re-inventing the game.  My wife even started to hate sea-themed board games because of this expansion. [Rating: 2/10] The unknown hexes that players can venture towards add another layer of randomness which can throw a wrench into a well executed gameplan or allow a haphazard gameplan to stumble into victory.   Personally, I found that this accentuates what I didn't like about Catan (the degree to which luck determines the outcome, rather than skillful play)

[Rating: 2/10] 220927 It makes Catan a little bigger but lacks innovation. A must to try, though. A first step to Expansions

[Rating: 2.5/10] Likes: About the only thing this offers is the gold tiles.  Dislikes: The sea tiles and thinning of the map just drags the game out. The trade/boat routes don't really offer much more.

[Rating: 3/10] Only played once - and I did'nt even have a go at it. So its heresay knowledge. Guess I'll never get to play this one. Keep it to complete my colection.

[Rating: 3/10] I love regular Settlers and Knights and Cities even more. This version, however, add no new fun over and above what you get with Settlers, but drastically adds to the setup and teardown time.  I would never choose this over regular Settlers or K&C

[Rating: 3/10] The added set up time and the scenarios just didn't do much to improve Settlers for me.  Cities and Knights is a much better expansion.

[Rating: 3/10] Takes what little I like about Settlers and ruins it.  I simply won't play with this set.

[Rating: 3/10] I like Settlers and Cities and Knights, but this expansion added very little in our games with it other than additional reading and setup time.  It has gold tiles.  That is about all the good I can say about it.

[Rating: 3/10] Doesn't add a lot to the basic game. Makes the game playable with 4 with the increased space, and gives you some room for variation to freshen it up. That said,  I think the complaint that it adds length without depth is fair. The option of much more random maps and the exploration variant are worthy additions in the abstract, but the reality of the implementation is not to my liking. I rarely get the urge to play Siedler anymore, and even more rarely with this expansion as the game plays at least 30-60 minutes longer because of the lack of 3 intersection hexes and longer roads/shipping lanes.

[Rating: 3/10] Hard for me to justify the added time this gives the game. Also it requires more than 2 players.

[Rating: 3/10] Owned the Mayfair 3rd edition (the one printed in 1998). In Jan 2014, I traded this and Cities & Knights of Catan and the 5-6 player expansions for both in return for Liberte and Perikles.  This one was a classic case of making an expansion for a game that didn't need one.  Still enjoy Settlers greatly, but its expansions were wasted on my groups.

[Rating: 3/10] Own Kosmos edition. It doesn't add much to regular Catan and rather prolongs the game in unnecessarily way. The main addition to the game is ships which are nothing but mobile roads on the ocean. It doesn't even travel. Not exciting at all. Only reason I have this is so that I can play some of the neat Senarios in Catan Book.

[Rating: 3/10] Doesn't add enough to justify its cost.  I haven't played with solely the Seafarer's expansion (typically with Cities and Knights as well), but I'd almost prefer to play normal Settlers.  Priced as much as the base game, I would never purchase Seafarers.  Maybe my rating is unfair, but I'm not sure if it adds anything particularly significant.  Only doubles the cost of the game.

[Rating: 3/10] As an expansion, it just added complexity and the game took a longer time to play. I did not enjoy playing with the expansion.

[Rating: 3/10] Seafarers allows for more scenario options, but otherwise I don't feel it adds much to the game at all. While C&K really gives you something more to chew on, Seafarers feels like nothing more than roads on water.

[Rating: 3/10] I love the visual aesthetics of building roads and shipping lanes.  The exploration scenarios carry no interst for me because the land tiles are so limited and mundane that there is no thrill in the discovery.

[Rating: 3/10] Game in a Nutshell: Expansion that creates water stretches that need to be crossed using boats to get to more settle-able land.  Played as: 3 and 4 player  Pros: The idea of sailing from one island to the next felt exciting.  Cons: I got pissed that it was the person who stuck to the biggest island, never sailed/ explored much, always ended up winning. I think you'd hope for an expansion to add something to a game, this seemed to break it.  Other: As I remember, there is a set up or two that has more, but smaller islands scattered around. [Rating: 3/10] Didn't seem to add much to the original Settlers.  I can't say it made the game worse, but why spend money to buy an expansion if it doesn't make the game better (or at least more interesting?) A big disappointment.
